links.outcome: Subgroup TPR/FPR disparities and accuracy after bias mitigation strategies versus naive model
links.effect: Reweighing nearly eliminated disparities (near-bias relative ΔTPR 0.44%, ΔFPR -0.69%); unlearning reduced them less (ΔTPR 12.22%, ΔFPR 15.51%); overall accuracy comparable to naive; unlearning hurt the no-bias dataset.
links.quote: The reweighing strategy almost perfectly mitigated any measured performance disparity between the bias groups, to respective values of relative ΔTPR and relative ΔFPR of 0.44 ± 1.80% and −0.69 ± 1.45% for the Near Bias scenario, and −0.80 ± 0.64% and −0.32 ± 2.13% for the Far Bias scenario.

links.outcome: Hidden subgroup performance gaps despite high aggregate accuracy
links.effect: Aggregate accuracy 84.81-87.68% across scenarios, yet relative ΔTPR 22.12% and ΔFPR 20.32% (Near Bias), 17.35% and 11.88% (Far Bias) between bias groups.
links.quote: The presence of the bias effect resulted in significant performance disparities compared to the No Bias scenario, with a relative ΔTPR of 22.12 ± 2.72% ( P <.0001) and ΔFPR of 20.32 ± 2.81% ( P <.0001) in the Near Bias scenario, and a relative ΔTPR of 17.35 ± 2.78% ( P =.0002) and relative ΔFPR of 11.88 ± 6.22% ( P =.0008) in the Far Bias scenario.

links.outcome: Model reliance on bias features (shortcut learning) from unequal group representation across classes
links.effect: With 70% vs 30% bias-group representation across classes, models used the bias effect as a shortcut, producing subgroup disparities.
links.quote: These results indicate that the models likely used the bias effect as a shortcut for predicting the (positive) disease class, since the disease class contains a higher proportion of the bias group compared to the non-disease class.
